title: Mann–Whitney U test
breadcrumb: Non-parametric methods → Two independent samples → Mann–Whitney U
engineName: Pool observations, rank together, compare rank sums.
objectives: Choose Mann–Whitney U for two independent ordinal-or-higher samples.
Pool observations and assign average ranks to ties.
Calculate both U statistics from pooled rank sums and verify their relationship.
State the null mean and variance, including the tie correction.
Interpret rejection without automatically claiming a median difference.

prereq.name: Independent samples
prereq.why: The groups contain different, unrelated observational units.

prereq.name: Ordering and ranks
prereq.why: The procedure replaces observations with positions in a pooled ordering.

prereq.name: Mean and variance
prereq.why: Large-sample inference standardises U using its null moments.

traps: Mann–Whitney is for independent groups; signed-rank is for paired observations.
Pool observations before ranking; do not rank groups separately.
U is not the rank sum R; subtract n(n+1)/2.
Tied observations receive average occupied ranks.
U₁+U₂=n₁n₂; this is not either individual U.
Rejection compares distributions generally; it is not always a median test.
howto: First pass: complete the pooled-rank worked example and both guided scenes. Revision: use the formulas, traps and revision sheet. Scope is two independent groups; paired observations belong to signed-rank/sign test, and three or more independent groups belong to Kruskal–Wallis.

sheet: Design: two independent samples; response at least ordinal; observations independent.
Pool N=n₁+n₂ observations and rank the combined list.
A tie occupying positions r,…,s receives average rank (r+s)/2.
U₁+U₂=n₁n₂; conventional two-sided statistic is min(U₁,U₂).
Z=(U−E(U))/√Var(U), with continuity correction if specified.
Median/location interpretation needs similarly shaped distributions.
cards: Distributional comparison; median shift needs common shape
tricks: Pool first, rank second, split rank sums last.
remember: Independent groups → Mann–Whitney; paired measurements → signed-rank/sign test.
Do not interpret every rejection as a median difference.

provenance: June 2026 Paper 2 Q42 anchor: two independent groups of 15 executives. Full 30 scores are ranked together using average ranks for ties. Exact-rank computation gives R_ES=152.5, R_LC=312.5, U_ES=32.5, U_LC=192.5 and min(U)=32.5. Checks: pooled rank total 465 and U sum 225. Verification independently sorts and assigns rational average ranks. Null mean, no-tie variance and tie correction are asserted. Candidate response details are excluded. The Q42 anchor tests the independent two-sample design and the U statistic. The ten module variants cover the observed U value, U sum, null moments, ties, pooled rank total, paired-test contrast, Kruskal–Wallis contrast, rank-sum conversion and ordinal scale. Q33 is a parametric test-matching item and is not treated as a Non-parametric anchor.

scenes.title: Start with the design
scenes.objective: Identify the sample structure before choosing a test.

ask.q: Two different classes use two teaching methods. Independent or paired?
ask.nudge: Does any student appear in both groups?

body: A test is chosen from how observations were collected. First decide whether groups are independent or whether each observation is linked to another. Then check whether the response has a meaningful order.

Mann–Whitney U compares two independent groups using the ordering of all observations. It does not require normal populations, but it does require independent observations and an ordinal-or-higher outcome.

items.ask: Two separate classes each use one method. What is the design?
items.recall: Two independent groups, if no student appears in both.
refresh: An independent-samples design uses different observational units in the two groups. A person, animal or item must not contribute to both groups. If the same unit is measured twice, the two observations are linked and the independent-sample rank procedure is not the right analysis. Identify the unit before selecting a test.

An ordinal scale has a meaningful ordering even when the distances between adjacent categories are not known to be equal. Satisfaction categories such as low, medium and high can be ordered. Blood groups cannot. Mann–Whitney uses the order of observations, so nominal labels alone do not supply the information it needs.

items.ask: What information does a rank preserve?
refresh: Ranking replaces a measurement by its position in an ordered list. The operation keeps which observation is larger and discards how far apart the two values are. For example, scores 51 and 52 are adjacent just as scores 90 and 99 may be adjacent; their numerical gaps do not enter the rank calculation. This is why the pooled order is central to the test.

A nominal variable consists of labels with no natural smallest-to-largest arrangement. Assigning numbers to labels does not create a meaningful order: coding blood groups as 1, 2, 3 and 4 would be arbitrary. An ordinal variable has a defensible order, such as mild, moderate and severe. The rank procedure requires that defensible ordering.

items.ask: Can nominal categories be ranked meaningfully?
items.recall: No. Nominal categories have no natural order.
refresh: When the same participant contributes a before score and an after score, those values are connected by participant. Treating them as independent would break that connection and discard useful design information. A paired method works with within-participant changes; Wilcoxon signed-rank and the sign test are common nonparametric choices. Use Mann–Whitney only when the groups really are independent.

A rank is not a standardised score and it is not a percentile calculated separately within each group. It is the position in the combined ordered sample. Pooling puts every observation on the same scale, so a value from group 1 can receive a higher rank than a value from group 2. Separate rankings cannot express that cross-group comparison.

scenes.title: Compare ordering rather than averages
scenes.objective: Explain why pooled ranks can compare two groups.

ask.q: If group 1 tends to have larger observations, where will its ranks lie?
ask.nudge: Think about the combined ordered list.

body: A few long waiting times can dominate an average. A rank procedure asks whether observations from one group tend to appear higher in the combined ordering than observations from the other group.

scenario.teaser: Two independent groups receive different teaching methods.
scenario.title: An executive training comparison
body: A training manager randomly assigns executives to two teaching methods. Each executive contributes one final score, and no executive appears in both groups. The samples are independent. Scores may be skewed and a few unusually high values could distort a mean-based comparison. A rank procedure uses the ordering of all scores without requiring normal populations. Independence remains essential, and the result must be interpreted with attention to the shapes of the two distributions.
scenario.q: What feature makes a two-independent-sample rank test relevant?
scenario.answer: Different executives appear in the two groups, so the samples are independent.

scenes.title: See the pooled ranking
scenes.objective: Assign pooled ranks and handle a tie.

ask.q: What rank do both tied values 8 receive?

viz.caption: Pooled ranks are assigned across both groups; tied observations share the average occupied rank.

body: Group 1 values are 4, 8 and 10. Group 2 values are 5, 8 and 12. Pool them: 4, 5, 8, 8, 10, 12. Positions are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The tied values occupy positions 3 and 4, so each receives rank 3.5.
Ranking each group separately would give each group ranks 1, 2 and 3 regardless of how high its values were. That destroys cross-group ordering.

scenes.title: The rank-sum and U formulas
scenes.objective: Derive U from a group's pooled rank sum.

ask.nudge: Use the total rank sum and subtract both minimum rank sums.

blocks.body: Let n₁ and n₂ be sample sizes, N=n₁+n₂, and R₁ and R₂ the pooled rank sums.
The smallest possible rank sum for n₁ observations is 1+2+…+n₁=n₁(n₁+1)/2.
U₁+U₂=n₁n₂. The conventional two-sided statistic is min(U₁,U₂); retain direction separately.

flow.title: Mann–Whitney workflow
flow.alt: Check design; pool observations; rank with average ranks for ties; calculate rank sums; calculate both U statistics; infer and interpret.
flow.note: Check the pooled rank total and U₁+U₂=n₁n₂.

scenes.title: Null distribution and ties
scenes.objective: State the null moments and tie correction.

ask.q: Which quantity is adjusted by the tie correction?
ask.nudge: The correction changes the variance, not the null mean.

blocks.body: Var(U)=[n₁n₂/12]×[N+1−Σ(t³−t)/(N(N−1))], where t runs over tied-group sizes.
Z=(U−E(U))/√Var(U). A continuity correction may subtract 0.5 from |U−E(U)| before division; follow the question's convention.
The general null compares the two distributions. A pure location or median interpretation requires similarly shaped distributions differing only by a location shift.

scenes.title: Guided calculation with unequal sizes
scenes.objective: Use the fixed-sum identity to find the second U.
scenes.problem: Two independent groups have n₁=8 and n₂=7. A calculation gives U₁=42. Find U₂ and the smaller U.
scenes.answer: U₁+U₂=56, so U₂=14 and the smaller U is 14.
scenes.check: The two values add to 56, equal to n₁n₂.

scenario.teaser: An ordinal outcome in two independent treatment groups.
scenario.title: A clinical comparison
body: A researcher allocates different patients to two independent treatment groups and records an ordinal symptom score after treatment. Each patient contributes one score and no patient appears in both groups. The response has a meaningful order, but equal numerical gaps between categories are not guaranteed. A rank-sum procedure is a reasonable candidate for a distributional comparison. If the same patients were measured before and after treatment, the data would be paired and Mann–Whitney would not respect that pairing.
scenario.q: What design change would make Mann–Whitney inappropriate?
scenario.answer: Using the same patients for both measurements would make the data paired.

solution.why: The two U statistics must sum to this value.
Subtract U₁ from the fixed total.

scenes.title: Six statements to challenge
scenes.objective: Detect common design and calculation errors.
scenes.intro: Decide true or false on all six before revealing.

items.claim: Mann–Whitney is designed for two independent samples.
items.why: True. Paired samples need a paired procedure.

items.claim: Each sample should be ranked separately.
items.why: False. Pool first so ranks preserve cross-group ordering.

items.claim: The two U statistics add to n₁n₂.
items.why: True. This is a useful arithmetic check.

items.claim: Tied observations should receive arbitrary distinct ranks.
items.why: False. Assign the average of occupied positions.

items.claim: The test always tests equality of medians regardless of distribution shape.
items.why: False. It compares distributions; a median interpretation needs common-shape assumptions.

items.claim: The data must be at least ordinal.
items.why: True. The ordering must be meaningful.

scenes.title: Transfer: choose the test first
scenes.objective: Select the correct rank procedure from a paired design.
scenes.problem: A company measures satisfaction for the same 12 employees before and after training. The response is an ordered five-category rating. Which procedure is appropriate, and why is Mann–Whitney not?
hints: Identify whether the same people appear twice.
A paired rank test uses within-person differences.
scenes.answer: Wilcoxon signed-rank is a paired rank procedure when assumptions are appropriate; the sign test is a more assumption-light alternative. Mann–Whitney ignores the pairing.
scenes.check: The cue is the same 12 employees measured twice.

solution.why: The two observations from one employee are linked.

solution.math: Within-person differences → signed-rank or sign test

solution.why: Treating paired observations as independent discards the design.

ask.q: Which design cue separates Mann–Whitney from a paired rank test?
ask.nudge: Check whether the same units appear in both conditions.

ask.q: Why is 'the medians differ' too strong as a universal interpretation?
ask.nudge: Two distributions can have different spreads but the same median.

blocks.body: Independent observations within and across groups; an outcome that can be ordered; and a sampling or randomisation design supporting the chosen reference distribution.
Evidence that the two population distributions differ under the null model. The difference may involve location, spread or other distributional features.

blocks.h: When a median statement is justified
blocks.body: If the distributions have the same shape and spread and differ only by a location shift, rejection supports a location and median difference. State this condition explicitly.

scenes.objective: Perform and interpret a two-independent-sample rank test.
body: Choose Mann–Whitney from the independent-sample design and ordinal measurement scale.
Pool observations and assign average ranks to ties.
Calculate R₁, R₂, U₁ and U₂, then verify both totals.
Use the null mean, variance and tie correction for large-sample inference.
Interpret rejection as a distributional difference; claim a median shift only with common-shape assumptions.

ask.q: What is the safest one-line rule for selecting Mann–Whitney?
ask.nudge: Two independent groups with an ordinal-or-higher response.
